# Instructions

This week, you worked with three new data types in R -- factors, strings, and date-times -- using the forcats, stringr, and lubridate packages, respectively.

In this milestone, you'll work with the declaration dates in `disasters` to find out whether disasters are declared more often in some seasons than in others.

To learn more about the variables contained in the data set, refer to the data dictionary: https://rstudio.github.io/academy-tidyverse-fema/assets/disasters_dictionary.html

## Data types

In this milestone, you'll extract the month of each declaration date and then create a variable that records whether each disaster was declared in the spring, summer, fall, or winter. You'll then plot the number of declarations in each season, in chronological order.

    +  Months 4, 5, 6 = "Spring"
    +  Months 7, 8, 9 = "Summer"
    +  Months 10, 11, 12 = "Fall"

(Hint: use function `case_when()` for recoding values of `declaration_month` into `season`.)

### Part 3 - The role of factor orders in visualizations

Now that you have a `season` variable, you can compute and visualize summaries for each season in the same manner as in previous milestones. Run the chunk below to view a summary table. It counts the distinct declarations (`disaster_number`) in each season, because one declaration can span many records.

```{r}
#| label: summary
seasons_summary <-
  disasters_seasons |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarize(
    n_declarations = n_distinct(disaster_number)
  )

seasons_summary
```

After you have run the chunk above to create `seasons_summary`, run the chunk below to visualize the data of `seasons_summary`.

```{r}
#| label: summary-plot
#| eval: false
seasons_summary |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = season, y = n_declarations)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Disaster declarations by season")
```

This is a nice plot, but the order of seasons on the x axis is arbitrary (alphabetical). Let's give the seasons a more principled order before we publish this plot.
